title: Conveyor Maintenance: 5 Signs You Need an Upgrade
excerpt: A guide to conveyor maintenance — the signs that precede failure, how to cost the delay, and when replacement beats repair.

faq.q: When does a conveyor need upgrading rather than repairing?
faq.a: When three or more signs appear together: mistracking that needs weekly correction, motor current rising for the same duty, difficulty sourcing spares, long changeovers, and increasing product damage. One sign on its own is a maintenance item; several together mean continued repair has become the more expensive path.

It is a structural signal, not a surface one: a frame out of square, worn or misaligned idlers, or a pulley no longer running true. Repeated adjustment treats the symptom while the belt edge wears against the frame and material spills at the point of drift.

faq.q: What does a minimum preventive conveyor maintenance schedule look like?
faq.a: Weekly checks of belt alignment and tension, monthly inspection of idlers and bearings for noise or heat, periodic logging of motor current against a baseline, inspection of transfer points for gaps or worn plates, and a defined stock of fast-wearing parts.

faq.q: Can conveyors be upgraded without stopping production entirely?
faq.a: Often yes, by phasing the work across planned shutdowns — particularly when the upgrade targets controls and drives while retaining the existing structure.

faq.q: How do conveyor speeds cause line stoppages?
faq.a: Mismatched speeds between units are among the most common causes of stoppages on lines whose machines are individually healthy. When a conveyor is not synchronised with the next unit's rate, product either accumulates or starves it, and the line behaves as separate machines rather than one system.

body:
Conveyor maintenance is preventive by nature: systems rarely fail without warning, they degrade until an unplanned stoppage forces the issue. The five clearest signals are persistent belt mistracking, rising motor current for the same load, changeover taking longer than the run, spare parts becoming hard to source, and product damage creeping upward.

Conveyor systems rarely fail without warning. They degrade — slowly enough that the people working beside them every day stop noticing, until an unplanned stoppage makes the problem impossible to ignore.

These are the five signals that most reliably indicate a system has moved past routine maintenance and into upgrade territory.

1. Belt tracking needs constant correction

A belt that drifts off centre and has to be adjusted every few days is telling you something structural. Persistent mistracking usually points to a frame that is out of square, worn or misaligned idlers, or a pulley that is no longer true.

Repeated adjustment treats the symptom. Meanwhile the belt edge wears against the frame, and material spills at the point of drift. When tracking correction has become part of the weekly routine rather than an occasional task, the frame and roller set are due for assessment.

2. Motor current is climbing for the same load

If your drive is drawing measurably more current than it did for an identical duty, something is resisting the motion — seized rollers, bearing wear, contaminated take-up, or a belt that has stiffened with age.

This one is worth watching because it is quantifiable and it precedes failure by a comfortable margin. A drive that is working harder is also running hotter, and heat shortens the life of every component around it. A simple trend log on motor current is one of the cheapest early-warning systems available.

3. Changeover takes longer than the run

Many older conveyor installations were designed around a single product at a stable volume. If your product mix has broadened since then, you may be spending a disproportionate share of the shift reconfiguring guides, adjusting heights and re-timing transfers.

This is a design constraint, not a maintenance problem, and no amount of servicing will resolve it. Adjustable guide rails, quick-release fittings and recipe-driven positioning are the kind of change that pays back in recovered production hours rather than reduced repair cost.

4. Spare parts are getting hard to source

When a control component is discontinued and the only supply is the second-hand market, your production continuity now depends on a scarce part. The risk is not gradual — it is a single failure away from an extended stoppage.

The same applies to a PLC that no longer has vendor support, or a drive whose programming software will not run on any computer you currently own. If restoring the system after a failure depends on knowledge held by one person, the exposure is real, and an upgrade to a supported platform is cheaper than the outage it prevents.

5. Product damage or spillage has crept upward

Rising reject rates at the end of a line are often attributed to upstream process variation when the actual cause is transport. Worn transfer plates, gaps at junctions, misaligned side guides and inconsistent speed matching between sections all cause product to tip, jam or abrade.

Because the damage is distributed across the line rather than caused by a single obvious fault, it tends to be absorbed into the accepted scrap figure. It is worth checking directly: inspect the product immediately before and immediately after each transfer point and see where the condition changes.

How to decide

One of these signs on its own is usually a maintenance item. Three or more together generally means the system has drifted far enough from its original condition that continued repair is the more expensive path.

The useful comparison is not upgrade cost against repair cost. It is upgrade cost against the annual value of the downtime, scrap and labour the current system consumes. Once that figure is written down, the decision is normally straightforward.

Conveyor maintenance: how to cost the delay

The right comparison is not upgrade cost against repair cost. It is upgrade cost against the annual value of what the current system consumes:

  • Downtime hours multiplied by the value of production per hour.
  • Scrap from product damaged in transport.
  • Labour hours spent on repeated adjustment and repair.
  • Spare parts replaced through accelerated wear.

Once those figures are written down the decision becomes arithmetic rather than judgement, and delay is frequently the more expensive option.

Transfer points: the most overlooked area

Most product damage originates at transfer points between conveyors rather than along the belt itself. The check is simple: inspect the product immediately before and after each transfer and identify where its condition changes.

  • Worn transfer plates scratch product or impede flow.
  • Gaps at junctions let containers tip or jam.
  • Misaligned side guides squeeze product in transit.
  • Height differences between belts create impact on transition.

None of these register as faults because none stop the line, so they persist for months inside an apparently acceptable scrap figure.

When replacement is the right call

Upgrading is not always best. Replacement makes sense when the structure itself is no longer serviceable, when the product mix has changed so far that the original design no longer suits it, or when added capacity requires re-planning the route entirely.

In those cases a new conveyor system designed around current requirements costs less than successive upgrades to a frame never intended for them. Our engineers can assess the condition on site before any decision — request a quotation, or see technical support.
